name_ar: أبو حامد محمد بن محمد الغزالي الطوسي
name_en: Abu Hamid Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Ghazali al-Tusi
summary: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (450–505 AH) was one of the most influential Muslim scholars of any period — a Shafi'i jurist, Ash'ari theologian, philosopher, and spiritual writer whose Ihya Ulum al-Din (Revival of the Religious Sciences) is one of the most read works in Islamic history. His intellectual journey from philosophy through a crisis of doubt to spiritual certainty shaped the integration of Sufism into mainstream Sunni Islam. Classical scholars differed significantly on aspects of his work: while the Ihya's spiritual guidance earned him the title Hujjat al-Islam, leading scholars including al-Dhahabi, Ibn al-Jawzi, and Ibn Taymiyyah raised serious concerns about specific hadith, theological positions, and Sufi concepts within his writings.
biography:
Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Ghazali was born in 450 AH (1058 CE) in Tus, in the Khorasan region of Persia (present-day northeastern Iran). He received early schooling in Tus and Jurjan before arriving in Nishapur to study with Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni (d. 478 AH), the foremost Shafi'i and Ash'ari scholar of his generation. He remained with al-Juwayni approximately eight years, establishing mastery of Shafi'i fiqh and Ash'ari kalam that would underpin all his subsequent work.

In 484 AH the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk appointed al-Ghazali to the head professorship of the Nizamiyyah madrasa in Baghdad — the most prestigious academic appointment in the Sunni world. He taught there for four years to packed audiences and during this period wrote his Tahafut al-Falasifah (The Incoherence of the Philosophers), a philosophical refutation of Avicenna and al-Farabi that targeted three positions he argued were incompatible with Islamic belief: the eternity of the world, divine ignorance of particulars, and the denial of bodily resurrection. The work established him as a serious philosophical interlocutor and was later challenged by Ibn Rushd's Tahafut al-Tahafut. (al-Ghazali, al-Munqidh min al-Dalal)

In 488 AH al-Ghazali experienced a crisis of spiritual certainty described in his autobiographical al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (Deliverer from Error): unable to achieve certainty through reason alone, he left Baghdad — ostensibly for Hajj, in reality for seclusion — and spent a decade of retreat and Sufi practice in Syria, Palestine, and the Hijaz. During this period he wrote the Ihya Ulum al-Din primarily in Damascus.

The Ihya Ulum al-Din (Revival of the Religious Sciences), in four volumes organized around acts of worship, social conduct, destructive character traits, and saving virtues, integrates Islamic law, spiritual psychology, and Sufi frameworks into a comprehensive guide to Muslim religious life. It has been read continuously across the ummah for nine centuries, from West Africa to Southeast Asia, in Arabic and in dozens of translations, and has shaped virtually every subsequent tradition of Islamic spiritual writing.

However, major classical scholars raised substantial concerns about al-Ghazali's works that must be presented honestly. Three recurring issues: first, hadith reliability — al-Hafiz al-Iraqi (d. 806 AH) wrote al-Mughni an Haml al-Asfar specifically to grade every hadith in the Ihya, demonstrating that a notable proportion are weak (da'if) or fabricated (mawdu'); this commentary is printed alongside the Ihya in standard editions. Second, theological positions — Ibn al-Jawzi (d. 597 AH) criticized what he considered innovated positions in al-Ghazali's Sufi writings; Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728 AH) criticized specific passages in the Ihya as inconsistent with the methodology of the Salaf; al-Dhahabi (d. 748 AH) acknowledged his greatness while identifying weaknesses and warning against uncritical acceptance of his positions. Third, the concept of kashf (spiritual unveiling) — some passages in Mishkat al-Anwar suggest that the purified heart accesses religious knowledge independently, a framework critics argued could displace transmitted revelation as the primary source of religious guidance. From an Athari standpoint, the concerns raised by Ibn Taymiyyah and al-Dhahabi regarding specific passages in the Ihya and Mishkat al-Anwar are substantive and should inform how readers approach those texts.

Al-Ghazali returned briefly to teaching at Nishapur's Nizamiyyah madrasa near the end of his life. He died in Tus in 505 AH (1111 CE). His title Hujjat al-Islam reflects the genuine breadth and reach of his scholarly contributions. Readers should engage the Ihya — and his philosophical and spiritual works generally — with awareness of both their extraordinary value and the legitimate classical concerns outlined above.
